overview.headline: Russia sale of Alaska in 1867 and its later significance

keyPoints.point: Russia kept fewer than four hundred permanent settlers in Alaska because it lacked financial and military resources.
keyPoints.quote: permanent Russian settlers in Alaska never numbered more than four hundred

keyPoints.point: Russia offered to sell Alaska in 1859 to counter British designs in the Pacific.
keyPoints.quote: Russia offered to sell Alaska to the United States in 1859

keyPoints.point: Secretary Seward agreed to purchase Alaska for $7.2 million on March 30, 1867, leading to Senate approval and formal transfer.
keyPoints.quote: on March 30, 1867, agreed to a proposal from Russian Minister in Washington, Edouard de Stoeckl, to purchase Alaska for $7.2 million

keyPoints.point: Alaska became a state on January 3, 1959, after gold discovery and later strategic recognition vindicated the purchase.
keyPoints.quote: Alaska became a state on January 3, 1959

keyTerms.gloss: conflict whose defeat reduced Russian interest in keeping Alaskan territory
keyTerms.quote: Defeat in the Crimean War further reduced Russian interest in this region.

keyTerms.quote: Beginning in 1725, when Russian Czar Peter the Great dispatched Vitus Bering to explore the Alaskan coast

keyTerms.gloss: Russian minister in Washington who negotiated the Alaska purchase
keyTerms.quote: on March 30, 1867, agreed to a proposal from Russian Minister in Washington, Edouard de Stoeckl, to purchase Alaska for $7.2 million

keyTerms.gloss: nickname for the Alaska purchase that was later vindicated by gold discovery
keyTerms.quote: Skeptics had dubbed the purchase of Alaska “Seward’s Folly,”
